newsitem.title: FRANCE: Train bomb triggers security alert across France.
newsitem.headline: Train bomb triggers security alert across France.

text.p: Hundreds of extra police took up position at key points in Paris and other French cities on Wednesday after a bomb tore through a Paris commuter train, reviving memories of similar attacks in France last year.

Two people died and 79 were wounded or in shock after the bomb -- bearing the hallmarks of Algerian Moslem militants -- hit the Port Royal underground station in the early evening rush hour on Tuesday. Seven were seriously injured, police said.

President Jacques Chirac called a meeting of top ministers to decide on the government response to the attack while officials pondered whether the bombing was an isolated act or the first in a new series of deadly attacks.
The meeting was to follow the regular Wednesday morning cabinet meeting at 10 a.m. (0900 GMT).
No one immediately claimed responsibility, but the target, the timing and the type of bomb recalled attacks last year by fundamentalists fighting against Algeria's French-backed military rulers.
Chirac, in a live television address, called the attack "a barbaric and terrorist act" and vowed that France would do everything in its power to fight terrorism.

Police chiefs drafted in 400 riot police and gendarmes and troops to put a security plan codenamed Vigipirate back into force immediately. Five hundred others were expected to join them later in the day.

The operation, applied across France during last year's wave of attacks from July to October, involved patrols by police, paramilitary gendarmes and soldiers at public transport stations, public buildings and in the streets.
Border controls, virtually eliminated under a European Union open border agreement, were reinstituted on Tuesday night.

The explosion occurred in the fourth carriage of an RER regional express train at 6.05 p.m. (1705 GMT) as it drew into the station on the Left Bank, near the sprawling Luxembourg Gardens and the Latin Quarter.
"We heard a big explosion. They told us 'get out, get out' but we couldn't breathe because there was so much smoke. It was panic, fear," said one passenger who was on the train.

The bomb was placed inside a 15 kg (33-lb) gas canister which had been packed with nails, similar to those used by the Algerian extremists last year when eight people were killed and more than 160 injured, justice sources said.
Investigators found fragments of the canister on the spot and the body of one of the victims had been mutilated by nails.
Yves Bonnet, a former head of France's DST counter-espionage service, said: "Only the Algerian Islamic Armed Group (GIA) threatens France with this kind of attack."

The blast at the junction of Boulevard Montparnasse and Boulevard Saint-Michel occurred just two stops away from the Saint-Michel station, where eight people were killed and 86 wounded in an attack blamed on Algerian extremists in July 1995.
About half of the wounded were on the platform when the device went off.

"I thought immediately about last year's bombings," said 20-year-old student Remy Jiemza. "There were women crying, people panicked, some people fell to the ground, others were bleeding. Everyone was suffocating."

An American resident in Paris who was walking past said: "I saw people pouring out of the train with blood all over their faces and jackets. The first policeman was there within a minute and the first ambulances arrived within 10 minutes."

France is also facing a bombing campaign by Corsican separatist guerrillas, who blew up Prime Minister Alain Juppe's Bordeaux mayoral office in October. But the outlawed Corsican National Liberation Front (FLNC) uses different explosives and usually takes great care to avoid casualties.

Following last year's attacks, dozens of suspected Moslem fundamentalists were detained across the country while police tracked down one small group believed responsible for a botched attack against a high-speed TGV train near Lyons.
